_comment: Shared ophthalmic steps. Used by the cataract, glaucoma, refractive, cornea, retina, strabismus, orbit and lacrimal operations.

step.eye.anaesthesia.title: Ocular anaesthesia: topical, sub-Tenon, peribulbar or general
step.eye.anaesthesia.why: The anaesthetic decides how still the eye is, how much the patient feels and which complications are possible. Needle blocks can perforate a long eye or bleed into the orbit; topical anaesthesia needs a cooperative patient and a gentle surgeon.
how: Agree the technique with the anaesthetist and the patient: topical (with or without intracameral local), sub-Tenon, peribulbar, retrobulbar, or general anaesthesia for children, long cases and patients who cannot lie still.
Read the axial length before any sharp-needle block: a long myopic eye or a staphyloma raises the risk of globe perforation, so prefer sub-Tenon or topical.
Check anticoagulant and antiplatelet status; a blunt sub-Tenon cannula is safer than a sharp needle if they are continued.
After a block, check for proptosis and a tense orbit (retrobulbar haemorrhage) before starting, and record the block, the drug and the volume.
pitfalls: A sharp-needle block in a long myopic eye.
Starting surgery on a tense, proptosed orbit after a block.

step.eye.povidone-iodine.title: Povidone-iodine 5% to the conjunctival sac
step.eye.povidone-iodine.why: Endophthalmitis is the infection that loses an eye after intraocular surgery, and the bacteria come from the patient's own lids and conjunctiva. Povidone-iodine in the conjunctival sac is the single antiseptic step with the strongest evidence.
how: Instil povidone-iodine 5% into the conjunctival sac and paint the lids and lashes with 5 to 10%.
Leave it in contact for about three minutes before the first incision or injection.
If the patient has a true iodine allergy (rare), use aqueous chlorhexidine 0.05% to the sac per local policy, never alcohol-based solutions.
pitfalls: Instilling it and starting immediately, before it has had contact time.
Skipping it because a topical antibiotic was given.

step.eye.lid-speculum.title: Microscope, lash drape and lid speculum
step.eye.lid-speculum.why: The lashes and lid margins carry the bacteria that cause endophthalmitis, and a poorly set microscope makes every later step harder. Isolating the lashes and setting the microscope before the first incision is part of the operation.
how: Set the microscope: patient's head level, the eye centred, focus and red reflex checked, foot pedal and the surgeon's posture comfortable.
Apply an adhesive drape that tucks the lashes and lid margins away from the field.
Insert the lid speculum gently, opening it only as far as needed, without pressing on the globe.
pitfalls: Lashes left free in the field.
Opening the speculum hard, which raises the eye pressure and pushes vitreous forward.

step.eye.biometry-iol-check.title: Biometry and lens implant check
step.eye.biometry-iol-check.why: A wrong lens implant gives a large refractive surprise that needs another operation. Most wrong-implant events come from the wrong patient's biometry, the wrong eye, or a lens picked from the shelf without checking against the plan.
how: Before the patient is in theatre, confirm the biometry belongs to this patient and this eye: axial length, keratometry, the formula and the target refraction.
Choose the implant model and power from the plan, plus a back-up lens for the sulcus if the capsule fails.
At the time-out, read aloud the patient, the eye, the implant model and power against the biometry printout; open the lens only after this check.
pitfalls: Using the fellow eye's biometry.
Opening the implant before the time-out check.

step.eye.intracameral-antibiotic.title: Intracameral antibiotic at the end of cataract surgery
step.eye.intracameral-antibiotic.why: Intracameral antibiotic at the end of cataract surgery substantially reduces endophthalmitis. The danger is a wrong dilution: concentrated drug in the eye is toxic to the retina.
how: Use the agent and dose of local policy, for example cefuroxime 1 mg in 0.1 mL or moxifloxacin, prepared and checked by two people or from a ready-made product.
Inject into the anterior chamber through the side port after the wound is sealed.
Record the drug, dose and batch in the operation note.
pitfalls: Preparing the dilution alone at the end of a long list.
Giving it to a patient with a true cephalosporin allergy.

step.eye.wound-check.title: Watertight wound and eye pressure check
step.eye.wound-check.why: A leaking wound lets bacteria in and lets the eye go soft; a pressure that is too high hurts and can close the retinal circulation. Both are found in seconds now and cost a great deal if missed.
how: Hydrate the corneal or scleral wound edges if needed and check that they hold when pressed gently.
Paint fluorescein over the wound (Seidel test) or watch for a leak while pressing beside it.
Feel the eye pressure with a finger or use a tonometer; aim for normal pressure, neither soft nor hard.
Suture any wound that leaks; one stitch is cheaper than endophthalmitis.
structuresAtRisk: Optic nerve and retinal circulation (pressure too high)
pitfalls: Leaving a soft eye with a gaping wound.
Overfilling the eye at the end.

step.eye.posterior-capsule-rupture.title: Bailout: posterior capsule rupture and vitreous loss
step.eye.posterior-capsule-rupture.why: A tear in the posterior capsule is the commonest serious complication of cataract surgery. Handled calmly it costs little; handled by carrying on as before it drops the nucleus into the vitreous and pulls on the retina.
how: Stop the phaco or irrigation: keep the instrument in the eye and inject dispersive viscoelastic before withdrawing, so the chamber does not collapse.
Tell the team. Lower the bottle height and the flow.
Remove any vitreous from the anterior chamber and the wound with an anterior vitrectomy (cutter, separated irrigation); triamcinolone stains it.
Do not chase a dropped nucleus into the vitreous: leave it for a vitreoretinal surgeon.
Place the lens in the sulcus (with optic capture if possible) or leave the eye aphakic, and record the event for the patient and the follow-up.
pitfalls: Pulling out the phaco probe and collapsing the chamber.
Sponge and scissors vitrectomy that pulls on the retina.
Chasing a dropped nucleus.

step.eye.suprachoroidal-haemorrhage.title: Bailout: suprachoroidal haemorrhage
step.eye.suprachoroidal-haemorrhage.why: Bleeding into the suprachoroidal space can push the eye contents out of an open wound within minutes. The response is to close the eye, not to keep operating.
how: Recognise it: the red reflex darkens, the chamber shallows, the eye hardens and the iris or lens comes forward.
Close every wound immediately with sutures, with a finger over the wound while the stitch is placed.
Tell the anaesthetist: lower the blood pressure, deepen anaesthesia and stop any coughing or straining.
Do not try to drain it at the time; record it, explain it to the patient, and arrange vitreoretinal review.
pitfalls: Continuing the operation through a darkening red reflex.
Leaving a wound open while trying to drain the blood.

step.eye.conj-peritomy.title: Conjunctival peritomy and Tenon's dissection
step.eye.conj-peritomy.why: Conjunctiva is the covering that protects a bleb, a muscle repair or an implant. A ragged or buttonholed peritomy leaks, scars or exposes what lies beneath.
how: Lift the conjunctiva with non-toothed forceps and open it at the limbus (limbus-based or fornix-based as planned) with blunt-tipped scissors.
Dissect Tenon's capsule from the sclera bluntly in the plane above the muscles.
Keep the conjunctival edges moist and handle them only with smooth forceps so they can be closed watertight.
pitfalls: Toothed forceps on the conjunctival edge.
Cutting through Tenon's into a muscle belly.

step.eye.conj-closure.title: Conjunctival closure
step.eye.conj-closure.why: A conjunctival closure has to cover what lies under it: a leak over a bleb drains the eye flat, and an exposed suture or implant becomes infected.
how: Lay the conjunctiva back in its anatomical position, edges flat and not inverted.
Close with fine absorbable sutures or tissue glue, anchoring to the limbus where needed.
Check for a leak with fluorescein where a watertight seal matters (over a bleb).
pitfalls: A gap at the limbus that leaks.
Inverting the conjunctival edge so it does not heal.

step.eye.refractive-check.title: Refractive surgery check: stable refraction, corneal safety and the laser plan
step.eye.refractive-check.why: Laser refractive surgery is elective surgery on a healthy eye, so the threshold for harm is very low. The two avoidable disasters are treating the wrong prescription and treating a cornea that will later bulge (ectasia).
how: Confirm a stable refraction for at least a year, from records, and a cycloplegic refraction where indicated.
Review topography and tomography for keratoconus or forme fruste keratoconus, and pachymetry for enough residual stromal bed.
Check the treatment plan in the laser against the patient, the eye and the refraction, and set the optical zone.
Confirm realistic expectations, contact lenses out for the agreed period, and no contraindicating eye or systemic disease.
pitfalls: Treating a suspect topography.
Entering the refraction for the wrong eye.

step.eye.excimer-ablation.title: Excimer laser ablation with eye tracking
step.eye.excimer-ablation.why: The ablation removes a precise depth of stroma to change the corneal curvature. Its accuracy depends on centration, a dry but not desiccated stromal bed, and a patient who keeps fixating.
how: Check the laser has passed its calibration test that day.
Ask the patient to fixate on the light; engage the eye tracker and confirm centration over the pupil or visual axis before firing.
Keep the stromal bed evenly moist and treat without pauses unless the tracker loses the eye.
Watch throughout; the surgeon's foot comes off the pedal the moment fixation is lost.
pitfalls: Firing without confirming centration.
A wet or dried-out bed giving an under- or over-correction.

step.eye.laser-interruption.title: Bailout: laser interruption, decentration or loss of tracking
step.eye.laser-interruption.why: A treatment that has gone off centre or stopped half way cannot simply be repeated from the start. Stopping cleanly and recording exactly where it stopped allows a safe completion.
how: Take the foot off the pedal as soon as the patient moves, the tracker disengages or the laser faults.
Re-establish fixation and centration; most lasers allow the treatment to resume from where it stopped.
If the fault persists, abandon the rest of the treatment, record the percentage completed, and plan completion after the cornea has stabilised.
Tell the patient what happened.
pitfalls: Restarting the full treatment after a partial ablation.
Continuing while the patient looks away.

step.eye.shield-postop.title: Eye protection, drops and the warning signs
step.eye.shield-postop.why: Most sight-threatening problems after eye surgery declare themselves at home: increasing pain, redness and falling vision mean endophthalmitis or raised pressure until proven otherwise. The patient has to know what to watch for and whom to call that day.
how: Apply a clear shield or pad as the operation requires; tell the patient to wear the shield at night.
Prescribe the post-operative drops (antibiotic, steroid, others) with a written schedule.
Tell the patient and carer in plain words: increasing pain, increasing redness or worsening vision means come back the same day, with a phone number that answers out of hours.
Book the first review at the interval the operation needs.
pitfalls: Discharging without a same-day emergency contact.
Drops written but not explained.
